text:
A vaccine lets the body rehearse an infection without the dangerous ending.

**Step 1: Showing the immune system the target.** A vaccine delivers pieces of a germ, called antigens. They can come from inactivated viruses, from purified protein subunits, or from mRNA that muscle cells in the shoulder (the deltoid) read and turn into protein. These pieces travel to the lymph nodes. There, dendritic cells pick them up and display small fragments, called peptides, on molecules known as MHC.

**Step 2: Training the antibodies.** Helper T cells are chosen from billions of randomly generated receptor types, and the right ones are those that match the displayed fragment. They signal B cells to multiply inside structures called germinal centers. These work like antibody boot camps. Over two to four weeks, small changes in the B cells' genes (somatic hypermutation) make their antibodies bind more tightly.

**Step 3: Keeping a memory.** Most of the fighting cells then die off. But long-lived plasma cells and reserves of memory lymphocytes remain for years, sometimes decades.

**The payoff.** When the real germ arrives, the second response starts within days. A first-time infection takes more than a week to get going. The body often stops the germ before symptoms appear.

**Boosting the effect.** Adjuvants made from aluminum salts have been used since the 1930s to strengthen the alarm signal. Booster shots quiz the immune system again, and immunity grows stronger.
